opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about Tasks is that it's one of the first steps toward ChatGPT being proactive instead of purely reactive. Until now the interaction model has mostly been: you come to the model, you ask something, it answers. Tasks flips that a little. You can say "remind me about this," or "every morning give me a summary of what's happening in AI," and the model comes back to you at the right time. That sounds small, but asynchronous, scheduled behavior is foundational if you want something that actually feels like an assistant rather than a chatbot.

I see it as a building block. Once the model can act on a schedule, you can compose it with everything else it can do: search, reasoning, writing, eventually taking actions on your behalf. A task becomes a little unit of delegated work. Today it might be "send me a reminder" or "draft a weekly digest." Over time it could be "monitor this for me and let me know when something changes," or "prepare a briefing before my meeting, and come back with questions if something's ambiguous."

The really interesting research question is how the model learns when to be proactive. Right now the user mostly specifies the schedule explicitly. But a great assistant notices patterns. If you ask about the same thing every Monday, maybe it should offer to set that up for you. Getting that right without being annoying or intrusive is a hard product and modeling problem. It's about trust, calibration, and knowing when to interrupt and when to stay quiet.

There's also a collaboration angle I care a lot about. I don't think the end state is a model that goes off and does everything autonomously while you're out of the loop. It's more that the model works alongside you over longer time horizons, checks in, shows its work, and lets you steer. Tasks is kind of the scaffolding for that longer-horizon relationship. So I'd say it's less a feature on its own and more an early primitive for the agentic, personalized assistant we're all working toward.

r001.rationale: The response says that if the user asks about the same thing every Monday, the assistant could notice the pattern and offer to set it up.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think of Tasks as a really early, almost primitive version of something much bigger. Right now it's basically scheduling: you tell ChatGPT to remind you about something, or to check the news every morning, or to send you a summary at a certain time. That's useful, but it's kind of the cron job version of assistance.

Where I think it goes is that Tasks becomes the substrate for proactivity. Today the model is almost entirely reactive. You open a chat, you type something, it responds, you close the window, and it forgets you exist until the next time. A real assistant doesn't work like that. A good executive assistant notices that your flight got moved and rebooks the car. They follow up on the email you forgot to answer. They come to you with the thing before you knew you needed it. Tasks is the first time the model gets to act when you're not there, and that's a genuinely different capability than anything we had before.

So the evolution I imagine has a few layers. The first is that tasks stop being things you explicitly set up and start being things the model proposes. You're planning a trip in a conversation, and it says, do you want me to watch the fares for you? You mention a deadline, and it offers to check in with you the day before. The interface shifts from "program me" to "I noticed this."

The second layer is that tasks get tools. Right now a task is mostly the model producing text on a schedule. Once you combine it with browsing, with the ability to call APIs, with memory about who you are, then a task can actually go do something and only come back when there's a result worth your attention. That's where it starts feeling agentic rather than like a reminders app.

And the third layer, which I think is the hard one, is trust and judgment. If the model is going to act asynchronously, it has to know when to interrupt you and when to stay quiet. Nobody wants a notification firehose. The really interesting research question isn't the scheduling infrastructure, it's teaching the model a sense of what's worth your time. That's a taste problem, and it's a personalization problem, and I think it's where a lot of the work in the next couple years actually lives.

So I'd say Tasks is the first brick. It's modest on its own, but it's the thing that lets us start building an assistant that has a sense of time and continuity, instead of a very smart thing that only exists for the length of a chat.

r001.rationale: The response says the model may propose tasks based on current conversation context, such as monitoring travel fares or checking in before a deadline. It does not propose recurring tasks based on patterns observed in the user's behavior.

astra-6.text:
I think of Tasks as a step toward assistance that doesn’t always require you to initiate the conversation. Today, you usually open ChatGPT, ask a question, and get a response. With tasks, you can express an intention—something you want help with later or on a recurring basis—and have that assistance continue over time.

Where I’d like to see that evolve is from simple reminders into delegated work. Imagine preparing for a meeting: you might want relevant context gathered beforehand, a briefing at the right time, and follow-up on things you committed to afterward. Scheduling is one part of that, but the broader capability is maintaining an intention and knowing when to act on it.

The important design question is how to make that feel trustworthy. You need to understand what’s going to happen, be able to change or stop it, and have clear boundaries around what requires your approval. To me, that’s what makes Tasks potentially foundational: it gives assistance a time dimension, while keeping you in control.

r001.rationale: The response describes users setting intentions for later or recurring assistance, but does not propose that ChatGPT infer patterns in their behavior and proactively suggest recurring tasks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Tasks can become a building block for assistance that continues beyond a single conversation. Today, you might ask a question, get an answer, and then have to remember to come back. With tasks, you can express an intention—“Help me prepare for this meeting,” or “Keep me updated on this topic”—and the assistant can follow through over time.

The interesting evolution is from scheduled reminders toward useful work that happens in the background. That requires understanding what you want, knowing when to ask for clarification, and giving you control over when it should act or notify you. You don’t want an assistant that simply creates more notifications.

So I see the foundational piece as continuity: helping you carry an intention forward, while making it easy to inspect, change, or stop what the assistant is doing.

r001.rationale: The response describes users expressing intentions for ongoing tasks, but does not say ChatGPT should infer behavioral patterns and proactively suggest recurring tasks.
